title: Signature generation fails for SM2 private keys with ES256 algorithm for node 18 version

qa_pairs.question: In auth0/node-jsonwebtoken 9.0.0 and 9.0.2, `jwt.sign(<payload>, <utf8 encoded SM2 private key>, { algorithm: 'ES256' })` fails on Node.js 18.17.0 with `"error":{"code":"ERR_OSSL_INVALID_DIGEST","library":"Provider routines","reason":"invalid digest"}`. The same command works on Node 16 but fails on Node 18 and 20. Is signing JWTs with an SM2 private key using the `ES256` algorithm supposed to be supported here, and if not, what is the expected support status?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says this is not supported: there is no registered JWS algorithm for SM2 keys, and `ES256` specifically requires an EC key on the P-256 curve. They also note that Node.js does not fully support SM2 keys. The bottom line given is that using SM2 keys with JOSE is unsupported and out of scope.
grounding_sources: IANA JOSE Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms registry

qa_pairs.question: The dependency tree for jsonwebtoken@9.0.1 shows semver@7.3.8. OSSIndex reports CVE-2022-25883 (ReDoS in semver new Range). Is jsonwebtoken affected and how should I remediate?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says the fix has been merged in PR #932 and released in version 9.0.2.

title: error:04075070:rsa routines:RSA_sign:digest too big for rsa key

qa_pairs.question:
I'm seeing `Error: error:04075070:rsa routines:RSA_sign:digest too big for rsa key` when signing JWTs with RSA algorithms in `jsonwebtoken` 8.5.1. For example, on Node in Windows I can get HS512 to work, but switching to RS512 or RS256 fails with:

```js
const jwt = require("jsonwebtoken");

const token = jwt.sign({ sub: 1 }, "...", { expiresIn: '7d', algorithm: "RS512" });
```

Another reproduction on Node 15 / Ubuntu uses this 512-bit RSA private key:

```-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
MIIBOgIBAAJBAKrNEPQdc2yJURauXDa2Yu2KLj6sHkM3EDMWrHEC/4RKdrMt9qFl
Hm11YoQRYIm2v/mtdBjrg+FD+MnaEtChYFkCAwEAAQJAX2YsqvzsJFpKVW3MCa8z
cFP24oCGYqqVvMNUS8cN6tgzm5XBZIuc7c2NQ+XzG7xGmvkklbTtKGCkBlrJHJ8L
AQIhAPfjw4kaK1RPga10Cc/+s4QGIRJUPsICBwVY2fFUDMk5AiEAsGOil+vUDr35
yMKod0NwCbUubukGHX/x6fxyY38G8CECIFtjM7Y62JiHizZIHkn5C3Nz0wNv3Ycm
ujHldMu8gc45AiEAg+6SP+WxoDEycpo+na4AUBKHn4eF/myjiis7d/YcP2ECIFnv
bdO+HrfCgkAcbMw0d2pEisYXfZWkAW8q9NJ4OyMp
-----END RSA PRIVATE KEY-----
```

with:

```js
const token = jwt.sign( tokenPayload, myprivateKey, { algorithm: 'RS512', audience: req.params.uid } );
```

and stack trace:

```
at Sign.sign (node:internal/crypto/sig:124:29)
aebc7411959c_web |     at Object.sign (/srv/www/node_modules/jwa/index.js:152:45)
aebc7411959c_web |     at Object.jwsSign [as sign] (/srv/www/node_modules/jws/lib/sign-stream.js:32:24)
aebc7411959c_web |     at Object.module.exports [as sign] (/srv/www/node_modules/jsonwebtoken/sign.js:204:16)
aebc7411959c_web |     at /srv/www/main.js:101:35
aebc7411959c_web |     at Query.<anonymous> (/srv/www/db.js:45:17)
aebc7411959c_web |     at Query.<anonymous> (/srv/www/node_modules/mysql/lib/Connection.js:526:10)
aebc7411959c_web |     at Query._callback (/srv/www/node_modules/mysql/lib/Connection.js:488:16)
aebc7411959c_web |     at Query.Sequence.end (/srv/www/node_modules/mysql/lib/protocol/sequences/Sequence.js:83:24)
aebc7411959c_web |     at Query._handleFinalResultPacket (/srv/www/node_modules/mysql/lib/protocol/sequences/Query.js:149:8) {
```

What is the relation, if any, between the RSA algorithm choice (`RS512`, `RS256`) and the modulus length of the key? Can I sign with `RS256` using a 2048-bit modulus, i.e. do the algorithm number and key size not need to match?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer explains that the modulus is part of the RSA private key and, for JOSE, it must be 2048 bits to be universally usable. A 512-bit key is insufficient; if you generate a 2048-bit RSA key, you can use all RSA-based signing algorithms. The `256` or `512` in `RS256`/`RS512` refers only to the hash algorithm, not the RSA modulus length.

title: Use a default of `["HS256"]` for `verify` to be in sync with default for `sign`

qa_pairs.question:
In auth0/node-jsonwebtoken, `sign` defaults to `options.algorithm: "HS256"`, but `verify` appears not to default to `options.algorithms: ["HS256"]`. Does `verify` accept all algorithms by default, including `none` and algorithms like `HS512`, and should `verify` require explicitly passing `algorithms: ["none"]` to accept unsigned tokens?

The behavior I observed was:

```js
> jwt.sign({ user: 42 }, undefined, { algorithm: 'none' });
'eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.'
```

Then verifying without explicitly allowing `none`:

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.')
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

And also when a false-y key is accidentally passed, e.g. an undefined env var:

```js
> jwt.verify('eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.eyJ1c2VyIjo0MiwiaWF0IjoxNTkzNDM2NTEyfQ.', process.env.MYKEY) // oops env var undefined
{ user: 42, iat: 1593436512 }
```

Also, by default `verify` seems to accept tokens signed with algorithms other than the `HS256` default used by `sign`, such as `HS512`. Is that intended, or should `verify` default to `algorithms: ["HS256"]` to stay in sync with `sign`?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer said it is false that `verify` accepts all algorithms by default: its default allowed algorithms are derived from the `secretOrPublicKey` argument, not from a blanket "accept everything" policy. For the specific `none` case, they said requiring `algorithms: ["none"]` explicitly was already tracked as a duplicate of issue #711. They also said accepting `HS512` when `sign` defaults to `HS256` was not considered a big deal, and that in the next major they planned to derive `sign`'s algorithm from `secretOrPrivateKey` the same way `verify` already does.

qa_pairs.question: According to RFC 7518 section 3.6, JWS objects "MUST NOT accept such objects as valid unless the application specifies that it is acceptable for a specific object to not be integrity protected." In `auth0/node-jsonwebtoken`, I can reproduce that `jwt.sign({'a':1}, 'asdf', { algorithm: 'none'})` produces a token, and then `jwt.verify(token)` returns `{ a: 1, iat: 1587359376 }` without throwing. I expected `jwt.verify(token)` to throw unless I explicitly pass something like `jwt.verify(token, '', { algorithm: 'none' })`. Is this intentional, and should there be some switch/options to require explicit acceptance of unsigned JWTs?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says `none` is not automatically accepted unless the developer provides no `keyOrSecret`, and that the three lines in the source are not the whole story. They also say they will consider making the `algorithms` option required when accepting unsigned JWTs in the next major release.

title: Less Secure (jwt token decodes without any secret)

qa_pairs.question: I created a JWT with `jwt.sign` using my own secret, then pasted the token into jwt.io and was surprised that it decodes without any secret and shows the username/password claims. Here is the demo token: `eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJ1c2Vybm1hZSI6InNzYXR5YW1jaGF1aGFuIiwicGFzc3dvcmQiOiJ3aHlpdGlzbWUiLCJpYXQiOjE1ODUxMzM0ODMsImV4cCI6MTU4NTM5MjY4M30.bKtmn03-ZnAAzNxnNk9ZPlrsbbk8lUThMt24gwL-r2w`. Is this secure for token-based authentication in a web app, and is there any way to encrypt the payload so it isn't readable without a secret?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer explains that `jwt.sign` signs a token; it does not encrypt it. JWT/JWS provides integrity and authenticity, so the payload can be decoded without a secret, while the signature is what gets verified. They also state that `jsonwebtoken` does not provide encryption, only signatures, and point to JWE/JOSE for encryption.

title: Add option to ignore signature validation (e. g. for dev/test purposes)

qa_pairs.question: In dev and test environments, I may need to work with a test JWT token that has no valid signature, for example when the token provider cannot be modified to create tokens in the way a relying party needs for a special edge situation. In that case I can manually modify the JWT payload to match/test the requirement, but the current `jsonwebtoken` implementation does not allow using this invalid token within `jwt.verify()`. Would it be possible to add a new `ignoreSignature` option to `jwt.verify()` (similar to `ignoreExpiration` and `ignoreNotBefore`) so that self-modified tokens can be used for tests while still checking `issuer`, `subject`, and `audience`? `jwt.decode()` helps decode the token, but it does not run those other verification checks.
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says it is too risky to add an `ignoreSignature` option to `verify()`, because without a signature the other checks do not make sense and the information cannot be trusted. They suggest solving the special edge case by fixing interoperability between the systems instead, and mention workarounds like mocking the token provider, using an abstraction around `.decode()` in tests, or re-signing a token for testing.

qa_pairs.question: I want to know why the `jsonwebtoken` package does not provide a `destroy` method to kill a token. I’m getting stuck trying to find the solution for how to set the expire time to `0` or the current time while logging out in a NodeJS app. How should I properly invalidate a JWT on logout?
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says the short answer is to keep a blacklist of tokens. They point to prior discussions in issues #375 and #626, plus an Auth0 blog post about blacklisting JSON Web Tokens and API keys for more background.

title: Security warnings reported for axios 1.15.0 dependency chain

qa_pairs.question: Our security scan reported warnings for axios 1.15.0: CVE-2025-62718 (High severity, CVSS 7.8) affecting axios, and follow-redirects@1.15.11 (Medium severity, CVSS 6.9) as a transitive dependency, with the scanner suggesting upgrading to 1.16.0. Is there a recommended axios version that already addresses this, or is a dependency update planned? Also, Sonatype OSS Index currently reports axios 1.15.0 as vulnerable to CVE-2025-62718 even though its description says "This vulnerability is fixed in 1.15.0."
qa_pairs.answer: The maintainer says Sonatype OSS Index is still reporting axios 1.15.0 as vulnerable to CVE-2025-62718, but their own description says the vulnerability is fixed in 1.15.0. They conclude this is simply a mistake in Sonatype's vulnerability database.
